summary: The month's most consequential evidence on AI-first schools came from journalists rather than evaluators: the New York Times reported that only 42% of Alpha School students met the company's own '2x' growth standard in both math and reading, and ProPublica and The Texas Tribune reported preliminary scores of 28% proficient in English and 10% in math at Unbound Academy, far below its charter projections and not yet published by Arizona. Federal policy kept loosening the measurement system a school model is judged by, with Ohio becoming the eighth state to receive an ESEA Returning Education to the States waiver on October 30, while the Charter Schools Program's eight new state grants put $416 million of start-up capital into play, $149 million of it in Texas. The ACT class of 2026 composite slipped to 19.2 with math flat, NAPCS's charter enrollment count and Arizona's official 2025–26 results were still unpublished on November 1, and a new Hamilton County experiment found AI hints help only when built into a structured practice workflow.

items.headline: Ohio becomes the eighth state with an ESEA 'Returning Education to the States' waiver
items.detail: Ohio may consolidate more than $38 million in federal funds through 2029, bringing the total across the eight approved states to more than $158 million. Its waiver also loosens Title III-A spending rules and the provider-list requirement for Title I direct student services. Earlier waivers went further on accountability: Indiana's (June 16) removed the requirement that academic indicators receive much greater weight, and Arkansas's (July 7) lets advanced students' high school test results count.
items.implication: Each waiver makes a school rating mean something slightly different from state to state, so a network expanding across state lines should plan to fund its own common outcome measure rather than rely on state ratings.

items.headline: AEI's tracker now holds 2025–26 chronic absenteeism data for 23 states
items.detail: AEI added California, Illinois, Indiana and Mississippi on October 30, up from six states in August. All of the first six (CO, CT, GA, LA, MA, RI) declined; AEI has not yet published a direction count across all 23.
items.implication: Attendance remains the input most school models can move fastest; once the 23-state picture is summarised it sets the baseline any model's attendance claim should be compared against.

items.headline: New York Times: only 42% of Alpha students met the company's own '2x' growth standard
items.detail: Working from internal learning data, the Times reported that only 42 percent of Alpha School students progressed twice as fast in both math and reading, the '2x' standard featured in the company's marketing. The figure is a reporter's reading of operator data, not an evaluation, and there is still no comparison group.
items.implication: Treat the '2x' claim as a target the operator misses for most of its own students, and make any grant to an AI-first design conditional on an independent comparison group, which no current public-school pilot provides.

items.headline: Randomized trial: a course-integrated AI tutor cut final grades by 0.37 SD
items.detail: In a trial of 2,379 undergraduates and 30 instructors across disciplines at one large U.S. public university, access to a built-in AI tutor reduced final grades by 0.37 standard deviations and learning-management-system participation by 0.90 SD among sections of the same course, with larger estimated losses for first-generation students. The authors read it as displacement of activities that already worked rather than a failure to teach. This is undergraduate evidence at a single site, not K-12.
items.implication: The strongest counterweight yet to the AI-first premise: a portfolio should require any AI-centred design to show it is not crowding out the instruction it replaced.

items.headline: ACT class of 2026: composite 19.2, math flat at 19.0
items.detail: 1,463,293 graduates had an ACT composite, up from 1,380,130. The mean composite fell from 19.4 to 19.2, math rose from 18.9 to 19.0 and 30% met the math benchmark (29% in 2025). ACT dropped science from the composite for tests from September 2025, so year-on-year comparison is imperfect.
items.implication: Alongside the SAT's gains, the ACT says high school math has stopped falling but is not recovering, which keeps secondary math a gap no proven school model has yet shown it closes at scale.

items.headline: SAT class of 2026 up 16 points; math still below 2020
items.detail: The mean total was 1045, a second consecutive year of gains with increases across all demographic groups. Reading and writing rose 7 points to 528, returning to pre-pandemic levels; math rose 9 points to 517, below the 2020 cohort average of 523. Forty-two percent met both readiness benchmarks among nearly 2 million test-takers.
items.implication: Math recovery is real but partial, and it is still the subject where a model has the most room to show a difference.

items.headline: 30 states have filed to join the federal scholarship tax credit
items.detail: The IRS list of states making an advance election under Section 25F for 2027 reached 30 as of September 14, 2026, under Revenue Procedure 2026-6. From January 1, 2027 individual taxpayers may claim a credit for contributions of up to $1,700 to approved scholarship-granting organizations serving low- and middle-income students.
items.implication: Demand-side capital at a scale philanthropy cannot match, aimed at private and microschool tuition rather than public-school seats, which changes who a new public school competes with for students.

items.headline: PISA 2025: U.S. math 463, flat since 2022, as OECD averages hit record lows
items.detail: U.S. 15-year-olds scored 463 in mathematics, not significantly different from the OECD average, with 35% below baseline Level 2 and 8% at Level 5 or above; reading was 490 against an OECD average of 461 and science 502 against 482. Across the OECD, reading fell 28 points and math 22 points between 2015 and 2025, and one in five students is now a low performer in all three subjects, up from 16% in 2022. The assessment covered 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies.
items.implication: International benchmarking has become a weaker argument for any model: the U.S. relative position improved because other systems fell, and U.S. math is still below its 2018 level.

items.headline: Charter Schools Program awards $416M to eight state grantees, led by Texas
items.detail: The FY 2026 state-entity grants, issued through the Department of Labor, total $416.1 million in expected funding: Texas Education Agency $149.2M, The Mind Trust $68.9M, Florida $53.9M, South Carolina $48.2M, Michigan $38.6M, Excellent Schools Washington $33.3M, Delaware $16.0M and North Dakota $8.0M. It follows the record $500 million CSP round of September 2025.
items.implication: Federal start-up money is concentrated in a handful of states, so philanthropic dollars there can shift from subsidising openings toward evaluating which new schools work.

items.headline: Gallup: satisfaction with U.S. K-12 education falls to a 27-year low of 32%
items.detail: Down from 35% in 2025 and 11 points in two years, with dissatisfaction at a record 67%. Parents' satisfaction with their own child's education also hit a low at 66%, against 32% for U.S. K-12 overall. Asked to rate schools area by area, a majority of parents gave an excellent or good mark in only one, preparing students to adapt to new technologies (51%); critical thinking drew 29% and preparation for work 27%. Walton Family Foundation/Gallup fieldwork, August 3-24, 2026.
items.implication: Demand conditions for new models are as favourable as they have been, and the areas parents rate worst, thinking and work readiness, are the ones hardest to evidence.

items.headline: LAUSD blocks generative AI on district devices for all students
items.detail: The restriction covers 2026–27 while a new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee drafts guardrails, with recommendations due to the board by the end of the school year. It reverses a policy that let students 13 and older use approved tools after digital-citizenship training.
items.implication: District policy is now a real deployment risk for any model whose instruction depends on student-facing AI.

items.headline: FY 2027 opens on a continuing resolution that expires December 11
items.detail: The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (P.L. 119-103) was signed September 2, 2026, funding federal agencies from October 1 until the earlier of December 11, 2026 or enactment of the regular appropriations bills.
items.implication: The federal statistics and evidence agencies a diligence process depends on, already mid-restructuring, now have ten weeks of funding at a time.

items.headline: New York City declares a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI, 2-K through grade 8
items.detail: Nearly 600,000 students are covered and AI features are switched off in the classroom tools they use, with exceptions for students with disabilities and English learners. High schools get twice-yearly AI critical-thinking modules, limited pilots and new screen-time limits.
items.implication: The largest district in the country has removed 600,000 students from the addressable market for student-facing AI through grade 8.

items.headline: Schools scramble after Gemini in Classroom opens to all ages
items.detail: Google's August 10 change lets admins enable Gemini for K-12 students of any age; safety vendors describe 'whack-a-mole' monitoring and Common Sense had flagged age-inappropriate responses.
items.implication: Vendor defaults are outrunning district policy, which raises the value of models that control their own stack.

items.headline: ProPublica and Texas Tribune: Alpha expands through vouchers; Unbound's preliminary scores far below projections
items.detail: After Texas rejected its charter bid, Alpha grew to more than 30 Texas campuses, most accepted into the state's voucher program, and now runs private schools in 17 states and Puerto Rico. Preliminary state scores presented to Unbound Academy's board showed 28% proficient in English language arts against a projected 65% and 10% in math against a projected 60%; Arizona has not yet published them.
items.implication: Demand-side funding lets an AI-first design grow without passing an authorizer, which shifts the job of demanding evidence from the state to funders.

items.headline: EdWeek's math tracker counts 22 states with math laws since 2022
items.detail: Nine state actions in 2026 alone, including automatic enrollment in advanced math in Arizona, Georgia and Iowa. Screening and intervention requirements are the most common elements.
items.implication: State mandates are converging on screening and intervention, which favours models that already embed both.

items.headline: First six states report 2025–26 chronic absenteeism; all declined
items.detail: Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts and Rhode Island posted declines; Rhode Island is within half a point of its pre-pandemic rate.

items.headline: Anthropic adds a district-managed tier to Claude for Teachers
items.detail: The free individual tier for verified U.S. K-12 educators launched July 14 with standards-aligned lesson planning, nine ed-tech integrations and no model training on teacher data.

items.headline: 35 states plus Puerto Rico now have official K-12 AI guidance
items.detail: AI for Education's tracker update; ExcelinEd counts seven states with enacted K-12 AI laws in 2026 and 20+ with active bills.

items.headline: NBER: two-year Khanmigo trial finds small math gains, low engagement
items.detail: In 18 Tennessee middle schools, assignment to Khan Academy with the AI tutor raised math achievement 1.3 percentile ranks per term (0.06–0.08 SD a year), similar to Khan practice without AI. 96% tried the tutor; the median student used it on a third of practice days.
items.implication: The cheapest AI bet, adding a tutor to an existing school, returns roughly 0.06 to 0.08 SD a year. That is the bar an AI-first redesign must clear.

items.headline: NBER: AI hints add value in math practice only when built into a mastery workflow
items.detail: A randomized experiment with more than 6,000 Hamilton County middle-school students found AI support slowed progress but improved accuracy after mistakes. Mastery progression alone did not raise scores a week later; the clearest delayed gains, marginally significant, came when AI was embedded in the mastery workflow.
items.implication: Evidence for AI as a tool inside a structured school, not for AI as the school: fund designs that specify the practice structure, not the model.

items.headline: Houston ISD converts two elementary schools to 'Future 2' schools
items.detail: From 2026-27, C. Martinez and Gregg elementary schools become pre-K-8 'Future 2' schools with a curriculum that prioritises interpersonal skills and real-world experience alongside core academics, staffed by teachers hired to support students working through AI-powered platforms. There are no academic requirements for admission and currently enrolled students carry over by default, with an opt-out to a nearby school. Scientific American reported the district pilots as tests of the Alpha School model.
items.implication: Corrected in November: the district's own materials say the first four hours follow its standard curriculum and only top-percentile students opt into the AI platform, so these campuses test a redesigned school day rather than the two-hour AI model.

items.headline: NWEA links chronic absenteeism to slower recovery, especially in math
items.detail: Across 2,000 districts from 2019 to 2024, high-absenteeism districts were about 50% further from recovery in math than in reading.

items.headline: AEI: absenteeism improved less than a point in 2024–25
items.detail: 22.6% of students were chronically absent across 45 states, down from 23.5%; only 29% of students are in districts on pace to halve 2022 rates by 2027.

items.headline: Education Department reaches 14 interagency agreements
items.detail: Four new agreements move special-education programming to HHS and civil-rights, privacy and desegregation work to Justice; Title I administration is shifting to Labor.
items.implication: The evidence and data infrastructure a diligence process relies on is being reorganised while it is being used.

items.headline: Gallup: only 18% of teachers get formal AI guidance
items.detail: 34% receive none; 48% only informal guidance. Fewer than 1 in 10 have formal guidance for any specific task.

items.headline: Microschooling sector analysis: half the sector depends on state choice funding
items.detail: The National Microschooling Center's 2026 survey of 1,000 microschools across all 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico finds one in five open six years or longer and 45% open three to five years. Half report that their families receive state school-choice funding and three in five rely mainly on family tuition, with 66% offering sliding-scale discounts. The survey does not settle the size of the sector; estimates of students attending still run from 750,000 to 2 million. For the first time, operators named growth in nonacademic learning as their most desired student outcome.
items.implication: A sector maturing in operations while moving away from measurable academic outcomes, so a funder wanting evidence here has to pay for the measurement as well as the school.

items.headline: Education Scorecard finds a U-shaped recovery and a 'learning recession' dating to 2013
items.detail: Math rebounded immediately after 2022; reading turned up in 2025 only in science-of-reading states; middle-income districts lag; 108 'districts on the rise' identified.

items.headline: Census: per-pupil spending hit a record $17,619 in FY 2024
items.detail: Up 6.6% from FY 2023, the final year of federal pandemic relief. Instruction was 58.8% of current spending.
items.implication: The cost baseline any new model is compared against, in the last year before relief funds expired.

items.headline: NEA: average teacher salary reaches $74,495; starting pay $48,112
items.detail: Nominal gains of 3.5% and 3.4%; after inflation, starting pay rose 0.7%. Fifteen states now average at least $50,000 for starting teachers, up from 13. The largest one-year raises were in Nevada (11.8%), DC (9.7%) and Delaware (7.6%).
items.implication: Staffing is the largest line in any model's unit economics, and it rose faster than inflation only at the top of the scale.

items.headline: RAND: student AI homework use jumps to 62%; 67% fear harm to critical thinking
items.detail: Use rose 14 points between May and December 2025, driven by middle and high schoolers.
items.implication: Student demand for AI is already universal; the open question is whether schools shape it or ban it.

items.headline: Pew: 54% of teens use chatbots for schoolwork; 59% see AI cheating as common
items.detail: One in ten do all or most schoolwork with chatbot help; 43% have used one to solve a math problem.
items.implication: Any assessment-based accountability claim now has to survive widespread unsupervised AI use.

items.headline: Charters added 111,349 students while districts lost 221,729
items.detail: NAPCS state-agency data show 39 of 43 state charter sectors growing. Over six years charters are up 15%, more than half a million students, while districts are down 4.4%, nearly 2 million.
items.implication: Growth for any model is now share-taking inside a contracting system, which raises the value of closures, facilities capital and conversions.

items.headline: Walton expands charter facilities fund to $400 million
items.detail: A $100 million expansion with Civic Builders and PNC. The fund now offers up to 100% financing and lends to schools open as little as six months. Since 2017 it has deployed $292.6 million across 33 loans and created 17,083 seats, at schools averaging 81% free or reduced-price lunch.
items.implication: The classic constraint on charter growth loosened rather than tightened, moving capital earlier than commercial lenders will go.

upcoming.what: NAPCS enrollment report and state charter counts
upcoming.why: Not yet published as of November 1 (last year's brief appeared November 14). Whether the charter-district divergence held for a seventh year sets the growth ceiling for every model in the portfolio.

upcoming.what: Arizona's 2025–26 report cards, including Unbound Academy's first AASA results
upcoming.why: The first official state-test evidence on the two-hour AI model with a non-tuition intake. ProPublica reported preliminary scores of 28% proficient in English and 10% in math; as of November 1, 2026 Arizona's report cards and assessment files run only through 2024–25. Last year's file was posted in October.

upcoming.what: AEI Return to Learn: additional 2025-26 state absenteeism data
upcoming.why: 23 states now have 2025–26 data. Whether the early declines hold across them decides if the sub-1-point improvement of 2024–25 was the floor.
Congress must pass FY 2027 appropriations or another CR. IES, NCES and the What Works Clearinghouse are inside the perimeter, mid-restructuring.
The first Nation’s Report Card since 2024 and the first fully post-relief snapshot; U.S. history and civics follow in summer 2027.
Whether real starting salaries keep pace with inflation.

upcoming.what: Education Scorecard (fifth edition) and NCES Condition of Education
upcoming.why: District-level recovery through spring 2026 and the official enrollment and staffing counts.

changes: Inaugural edition compiled from primary sources published through September 4, 2026.
Baseline series established: NAEP 2013–2024, chronic absenteeism 2018–2025, enrollment 2019–2024, TIMSS 2015–2023.
Added the evidence register: nonprofits with randomized-trial evidence, sorted by ESSA tier, plus a watch lane of approaches still under evaluation.

Rebuilt for a program director investing in school models: added the School models and Conditions for scale sections, reframed the landscape, AI and foundations sections around that reader, and added an implication line to each briefing item.
Retired the standalone intervention register; its rows now sit inside Academic foundations, and BARR moved to the school models lane.
Added PISA 2025 to Academic foundations as two paired blocks, the U.S. result and the OECD picture, with the standing-still caveat stated in the lede and the recovery findings.

School models: Alpha School row updated for the Houston ISD Future 2 conversions, the first non-selective district test of the two-hour model; microschools row and KPI rebuilt on the Center’s 2026 sector analysis.

Added the October 2026 randomized trial of a course-integrated AI tutor (−0.37 SD on final grades) to the AI evidence table, the school-models findings and a new "where the field disagrees" entry alongside the Khanmigo trial.
Conditions for scale: added the Section 25F scholarship tax credit (30 states, 2027 start) to the capital table and the FY 2027 continuing resolution to the funding picture.
Landscape: Gallup satisfaction 35% → 32% (new 27-year low) and the SAT class of 2026 (1045, math 517).

Left unchanged for want of a newer primary source: NAEP 2024, CREDO NCSS3, KIPP and BARR effects, NAPCS enrollment, IES restructuring, Walton and City Fund capital figures. Unbound Academy’s first-year state results could not be verified on a primary source and are not on the dashboard.

Verification pass after the network policy was opened: re-checked the October figures against the publishers’ own pages and data files (NCES PISA 2025 data, Gallup, College Board, IRS, govinfo, EdWorkingPapers, the Microschooling Center, the NAEP data service).
Corrected the microschool student range from 750,000–2.1 million back to 750,000–2 million: the higher bound does not appear on the Center’s own pages.
Removed the House vote count on the continuing resolution, which is not in the enacted text; dated the Gallup (Sept 7) and SAT (Sept 29) items precisely.
Unbound Academy: confirmed from Arizona’s own report-card system that 2025–26 results are not yet published there, and said so in the row.

School models: Alpha School row updated with the New York Times finding (42% met the operator's own '2x' standard in both subjects) and ProPublica/Texas Tribune's Texas Preparatory School comparison; Unbound Academy row now quotes the preliminary 28% ELA and 10% math proficiency reported by ProPublica, labelled as unpublished by the state. Tiers unchanged: no independent evaluation has published.

Correction: the Alpha School row, the school-models finding and the August Houston briefing item no longer describe Houston ISD's Future 2 campuses as a non-selective test of the two-hour AI model. HISD's own announcement and its April 28 'For the Record' post say the first four hours follow the district's standard curriculum, only top-percentile MAP students opt into the AI platform, and AI does not deliver instruction independently.
School models and Conditions for scale: added the FY 2026 Charter Schools Program state-entity grants ($416.1M, eight grantees) to the funder chips and the capital table.

Conditions for scale: replaced the 'More waivers' KPI with a count of ESEA Returning Education to the States waivers (8, Ohio on October 30) and rewrote the flexibility finding around the Indiana and Arkansas accountability changes; the AI-first disagreement entry now carries the NYT figure.
AI and learning: added the NBER Hamilton County mastery-practice experiment (Working Paper 35621) to the evidence table.

Landscape and math: ACT class of 2026 (composite 19.2, math 19.0, 30% meeting the math benchmark) added to the graduation tile note and the math findings; AEI absenteeism tile now counts 23 states with 2025–26 data.

Pruned briefing items older than four months that no longer source a headline figure (Texas STAAR, Common Sense census, NWEA recovery, FY 2026 appropriations, City Fund and Bloomberg, the 2025 waiver letter); their figures remain in the section files.

Left unchanged for want of a newer primary source: NAPCS charter enrollment (2025 brief), CREDO NCSS3, KIPP and BARR effects, NAEP 2024, PDK 2025, Walton and City Fund capital, IES restructuring status, the 30-state scholarship tax credit count. Arizona has not published Unbound Academy's 2025–26 results.
